Methods: Valid data were obtained from a preregistered online cross-sectional study of 938 prediction market users via Prolific in late 2026.

Participants were compensated 0.25 GBP (≈ 0.34 USD) for completing a 1-minute pre-screen questionnaire 1 As per REB protocols, the dataset includes the 944 participants who consented to their data being uploaded to the Open Science Framework.
Participants were eligible for the present study if they were: 18 years of age or older, fluent in English, resided in the United States, and had traded on prediction markets in the past 12 months.
A total of 5,137 participants completed the prescreen questionnaire.
Overall, 1,005 prescreened participants were eligible and proceeded to the full survey.
All participants provided informed consent and upon completion, participants were debriefed and compensated 3.50 GBP (≈ 4.69 USD).

Participants were also asked: "In the past 12 months, how often have you bet or traded contracts on a prediction market?", if they selected "never" they were directed to the end of the survey (n = 18).

For those who passed this eligibility check and completed the full survey (N = 987), participants were excluded from analysis if they: (1) endorsed using a fictitious prediction markets website ("AsPredicted"; n = 21), (2) failed an attention check embedded in the Positive Play Scale (n = 32), and/or (3) indicated that their answers were "not at all accurate" (n = 0).

Participants were asked to list their top three reasons for using prediction markets using an open-ended text box, as well as their top three reasons for using prediction markets to purchase sporting event contracts instead of betting on traditional sports books.

Participants were also asked to rate on a Likert scale from 1 (Never or almost never) to 4 (Always or almost always) to what extent they trade on prediction markets for the following reasons: excitement, coping, social, financial, knowledge, accomplishment, social recognition, and amotivation (i.e., without a clear reason or goal) with higher ratings on each item indicating greater endorsement of that motivation.

Participants were asked two open-response questions about their general prediction market motives ("Please describe your top three motivations for using prediction markets?"), as well as their reasons for using prediction markets over conventional Sportsbook websites ("When you have the option to bet/trade on sports on both prediction markets and sportsbook websites (e.g., FanDuel, DraftKings), what are your reasons for using prediction markets instead of sportsbook websites?").
For each question, participants were asked to provide their top three motivations.
However, participants were more likely to perceive prediction markets as a form of gambling than as a form of trading, t(937) = 19.72, p <.001, d = 0.64.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Careless Responding

2 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Respondent = c("FL_36", "FL_36"), "Blocks flagged" = c(9L, 
5L), Scales = c("gambl_descrip_2 (1-6, 10 items); gmqf (1-4, 8 items); k10 (1-5, 10 items); pgsi (0-3, 9 items); pos_play (1-7, 5 items); pos_play (1-7, 9 items); predic_mark_4 (1-6, 7 items); predic_mark_8 (1-4, 8 items); supps_p (1-4, 20 items)",

), "Longest run" = c("same answer 20 times in a row, out of 20 items (flagged at 16)", 
"same answer 20 times in a row, out of 20 items (flagged at 16)"
), "Short-scale only" = c("no", "no")), row.names = 2:1, class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
```

**What this does not cover.** Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Methods: Valid data were obtained from a preregistered online cross-sectional study of 938 prediction market users via Prolific in late 2026.

Participants were compensated 0.25 GBP (≈ 0.34 USD) for completing a 1-minute pre-screen questionnaire 1 As per REB protocols, the dataset includes the 944 participants who consented to their data being uploaded to the Open Science Framework.
Participants were eligible for the present study if they were: 18 years of age or older, fluent in English, resided in the United States, and had traded on prediction markets in the past 12 months.
A total of 5,137 participants completed the prescreen questionnaire.
Overall, 1,005 prescreened participants were eligible and proceeded to the full survey.
All participants provided informed consent and upon completion, participants were debriefed and compensated 3.50 GBP (≈ 4.69 USD).

Participants were also asked: "In the past 12 months, how often have you bet or traded contracts on a prediction market?", if they selected "never" they were directed to the end of the survey (n = 18).

For those who passed this eligibility check and completed the full survey (N = 987), participants were excluded from analysis if they: (1) endorsed using a fictitious prediction markets website ("AsPredicted"; n = 21), (2) failed an attention check embedded in the Positive Play Scale (n = 32), and/or (3) indicated that their answers were "not at all accurate" (n = 0).

Participants were asked to list their top three reasons for using prediction markets using an open-ended text box, as well as their top three reasons for using prediction markets to purchase sporting event contracts instead of betting on traditional sports books.

Participants were also asked to rate on a Likert scale from 1 (Never or almost never) to 4 (Always or almost always) to what extent they trade on prediction markets for the following reasons: excitement, coping, social, financial, knowledge, accomplishment, social recognition, and amotivation (i.e., without a clear reason or goal) with higher ratings on each item indicating greater endorsement of that motivation.

Participants were asked two open-response questions about their general prediction market motives ("Please describe your top three motivations for using prediction markets?"), as well as their reasons for using prediction markets over conventional Sportsbook websites ("When you have the option to bet/trade on sports on both prediction markets and sportsbook websites (e.g., FanDuel, DraftKings), what are your reasons for using prediction markets instead of sportsbook websites?").
For each question, participants were asked to provide their top three motivations.
However, participants were more likely to perceive prediction markets as a form of gambling than as a form of trading, t(937) = 19.72, p <.001, d = 0.64.
Lastly, our sample was recruited from Prolific, which may limit generalizability of our results compared to population-representative samples (Pickering & Blaszczynski, 2021).

text.text: Background and Aims: Prediction markets have exploded in popularity since a 2024 US court case concluded they should be regulated as financial products, even when used to wager on sport event outcomes.
This study therefore explored the convergence of prediction markets and traditional forms of gambling, in particular sports betting.

Specifically, we explored whether higher rates of prediction market use would associate with demographic (i.e., age, sex, income, education) and psychological (i.e., impulsivity, financially focused self-concept, psychological distress, problematic alcohol/cannabis use) predictors of problem gambling, alongside direct measures of problem gambling (e.g., Problem Gambling Severity Index [PGSI], Gambling Fallacies Measure [GFM], and Positive Play Scale [PPS]).
Participants' motivations for using prediction markets were obtained via free-text responses.
Methods: Valid data were obtained from a preregistered online cross-sectional study of 938 prediction market users via Prolific in late 2026.
A Cochran's Q test and a z-test explored whether most participants used prediction markets for sports betting and also engaged with conventional gambling products.
Ordinal logistic models explored whether higher rates of selfreported prediction market use correlated with demographic, psychological, and gambling predictors of interest.
Qualitative inductive content analysis explored participants' motivations.
Results: As hypothesised, sports contracts were the most popular (81.2%), which was significantly greater than the next most popular category of financial events (55.2%,p<.001).

text.text: As hypothesised, younger age (OR=1.02,p=.048) and being male (OR=1.39, p=.048) were associated with greater prediction market frequency.
However, income was not (LRχ²(7)=13.49, p=.061).

Being more educated was significantly associated with greater prediction market frequency overall (LRχ²(4)=11.85,p=.025); although no individual category PREDICTION MARKETS AND GAMBLING differed from its reference group.

As hypothesised, higher scores on four out of five facets of impulsivity (x 2 (1)=8.25-22.67,ps<.005), higher financially focused self-concept (x 2 (1)=13.02,p<.001), higher psychological distress (x 2 (1)=4.11,p<.001), and higher problematic alcohol (x 2 (1)=15.42,p<.001) and cannabis use (x 2 (1)=15.71,p<.001) were all associated with greater prediction market use, as was higher PGSI (x 2 (1)=93.30,p<.001), lower PPS (x 2 (1)=32.99-65.09,p<.001), but lower GFM was contrastingly not (x 2 (1)=3.84,p=.050).

text.text: Participants most commonly reported using prediction markets to win money (52.54%), and reported using them over conventional sportsbooks due to better user-interfaces (36.58%).
Conclusion: US-based prediction market users fit many hallmark characteristics of conventional gambling users, questioning prediction markets' regulation as financial products.
The prediction market sector has grown rapidly since the US federal court ruled in favour of political event contracts in 2024 (KalshiEx v. CFTC, 2024).
text.formatted: The prediction market sector has grown rapidly since the US federal court ruled in favour of political event contracts in 2024 <ref type="bibr">(KalshiEx v. CFTC, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Monthly global trading volume on the two largest prediction markets, Kalshi and Polymarket, has surged from less than $2 billion in May 2025 to roughly $26 billion in May 2026, and reached $53 billion during the soccer World Cup in July 2026 (Radde, 2026).

text.text: Prediction markets allow users to purchase event contracts (i.e., positions on whether a real-world event will occur) ranging from election results to millimetres of rain in a given week.
A contract resolves when the event concludes, with those who purchased the correct outcome receiving the full contract value per share, paid for by those who bet on the incorrect outcome.
Lower-probability trade positions cost less to purchase and therefore pay out more if they resolve in the holder's favour.
The platforms themselves do not set the odds; the price of a given contract fluctuates with user supply and demand, with platforms collecting a transaction fee.
Thus, prices reflect users' aggregate probability estimates of an outcome (i.e., the wisdom of crowds; Surowiecki, 2005).
text.formatted: Thus, prices reflect users' aggregate probability estimates of an outcome (i.e., the wisdom of crowds; <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Surowiecki, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: This peer-to-peer structure, where users are essentially betting against each other, facilitates financial functions (e.g., risk hedging and price discovery), meaning that prediction markets can serve useful economic functions by providing consensus probability estimates of for example whether the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates (Rabinovitz & Packin, 2025).
text.formatted: This peer-to-peer structure, where users are essentially betting against each other, facilitates financial functions (e.g., risk hedging and price discovery), meaning that prediction markets can serve useful economic functions by providing consensus probability estimates of for example whether the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Rabinovitz & Packin, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, other popular prediction market outcomes have less economic value and look more like gambling, such as predictions of how many times Elon Musk will post on X in a given week or the outcome of an upcoming NFL game (Andrade & Newall, 2025).
text.formatted: However, other popular prediction market outcomes have less economic value and look more like gambling, such as predictions of how many times Elon Musk will post on X in a given week or the outcome of an upcoming NFL game <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Andrade & Newall, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Of importance to the present study, it has been argued that prediction markets are indeed a form of gambling, with several states (e.g., Minnesota, Utah) moving to restrict or outright ban them on these grounds (Allyn, 2026a).

text.text: Both prediction markets and gambling involve staking money on uncertain future outcomes, with losses and gains dependent on whether those outcomes occur (Johnson & Chan, 2026).
text.formatted: Both prediction markets and gambling involve staking money on uncertain future outcomes, with losses and gains dependent on whether those outcomes occur <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Johnson & Chan, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Further, as the range of event contracts grows, and in particular fast-resolving events, prediction markets become an increasingly continuous experience that resembles many high-risk forms of traditional gambling, such as electronic gaming machines (Allami et al., 2021; Johnson & Chan, 2026).
text.formatted: Further, as the range of event contracts grows, and in particular fast-resolving events, prediction markets become an increasingly continuous experience that resembles many high-risk forms of traditional gambling, such as electronic gaming machines <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allami et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Johnson & Chan, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Sports betting is perhaps the most notable convergence between prediction markets and traditional gambling, with direct overlap in available events.
Consequently, it is not surprising that 58% of prediction market users who had purchased sports contracts acknowledged that they were effectively gambling (Mastromartino, 2026).
text.formatted: Consequently, it is not surprising that 58% of prediction market users who had purchased sports contracts acknowledged that they were effectively gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Mastromartino, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this evident convergence, current US policy classifies prediction markets as a financial product, not gambling (Rabinovitz & Packin, 2025).
text.formatted: Despite this evident convergence, current US policy classifies prediction markets as a financial product, not gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Rabinovitz & Packin, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence of whether prediction markets are effectively another form of gambling can be obtained by observing whether or not highly-engaged prediction market users fit the demographic and psychological profiles that have been associated with an increased risk of suffering from problem gambling severity.

For example, financially focused self-concept, impulsivity, and psychological distress have each been associated with increased problem gambling severity (Haw, 2017; Tabri et al., 2017; Yeung et al., 2025), as have problematic alcohol and cannabis use (Armoon et al., 2025; McGrath et al., 2023).

text.text: Furthermore, problematic gambling severity has been correlated with fallacious beliefs about how chance works (Leonard & Williams, 2016), and has been correlated with risky behaviors (Wood et al., 2017).

text.text: We therefore preregistered the following hypotheses.

We hypothesised that sports event contracts would be the most popular contracts among prediction market event contract categories (sports, domestic politics, international politics, geopolitical conflicts, financial markets or futures, awards, and other) (H1), and that most prediction market users would also report engaging in traditional gambling activities (e.g., electronic gambling machines, lottery or raffle/scratch tickets, poker; H2).
Across demographics, psychological characteristics, and mental health and substance use, higher frequency of prediction market use would resemble patterns seen in traditional sports bettors (H3).
Demographically, higher frequency of prediction market use would be associated with being young, highly educated, male, and having higher income (H3a).
Psychologically, higher frequency of prediction market use would be positively correlated with greater impulsivity and financially focused self-concept (H3b).

Higher frequencies of prediction market use would be positively correlated with greater psychological distress, higher rates of problematic cannabis use, and higher rates of problematic alcohol use (H3c).
text.formatted: Higher frequencies of prediction market use would be positively correlated with greater psychological distress, higher rates of problematic cannabis use, and higher rates of problematic alcohol use <ref type="bibr">(H3c)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, we hypothesized that among prediction market users, that higher frequency of prediction market use would be associated with greater gambling-related risk and harm, including higher problem gambling severity, greater endorsement of gambling fallacies, and lower positive play (H4).
These quantitative tests were complemented by an exploratory qualitative analysis of free-text responses given to two items regarding participants' motivations for using prediction markets.

Participants were eligible for the present study if they were: 18 years of age or older, fluent in English, resided in the United States, and had traded on prediction markets in the past 12 months.

The median survey length was 20:50.

Participants were also asked: "In the past 12 months, how often have you bet or traded contracts on a prediction market?", if they selected "never" they were directed to the end of the survey (n = 18).

For those who passed this eligibility check and completed the full survey (N = 987), participants were excluded from analysis if they: (1) endorsed using a fictitious prediction markets website ("AsPredicted"; n = 21), (2) failed an attention check embedded in the Positive Play Scale (n = 32), and/or (3) indicated that their answers were "not at all accurate" (n = 0).

Approximately 84% of participants (n = 788) reported engaging in traditional forms of gambling in the past 12 months, and 80.5% of participants (n = 755) reported trading on financial markets.

Approximately 395 (42.1%) participants resided in states where online sports betting was illegal or limited, with California (n = 102, 10.9%), Texas (n = 82, 8.7%), and Florida (n = 79, 8.4%) being the three most reported states of residence.

We also assessed the platforms (e.g., Kalshi) used to trade.
The perception of prediction markets as either gambling or financial trading was measured using two items.
Each item was rated on a Likert scale from 0 (not at all) to 10 (completely), with higher ratings indicating greater endorsement of that belief.
Motivations for prediction market use were assessed qualitatively and quantitatively.

Participants were asked to list their top three reasons for using prediction markets using an open-ended text box, as well as their top three reasons for using prediction markets to purchase sporting event contracts instead of betting on traditional sports books.

Analyses were conducted in SPSS, version 31.
To test H1, participant endorsement of event contracts purchased across event categories was analyzed using Cochran's Q test.
Following a significant Cochran's Q test, post-hoc pairwise McNemar tests with False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction were used to determine which categories differed significantly from sports events.
Where significant differences were found, the category with the higher endorsement proportion was identified as more popular.
To test H2, the proportion of prediction market users who also reported engaging in gambling activities was analyzed using a onesample, one-tailed z-test for proportions.
To test H3 and H4, ordinal logistic regressions were conducted, with frequency of prediction market trades as the outcome and each variable of interest modelled as a separate predictor.

FDR correction was applied separately within each family of tests (demographic [separately for those in the pre-registered and exploratory analysis], psychological characteristics, mental health and substance use, and measures of gambling-related harm).
For all statistical tests, an FDR-adjusted p-value < .05 was considered significant.

text.text: Quantitative exploratory analyses included two separate one-sample t tests that were used to examine whether participants' perception of prediction markets as a form of gambling and as a form of trading were significantly higher than each scale's midpoint of 5.
A paired-samples t test was also used to test the difference in scores between these scales.

Additionally, gender, sexual orientation, relationship status, employment, and ethnicity were examined using separate ordinal logistic regressions; frequency of prediction market trades served as the outcome and each demographic variable was modeled as a predictor.
These variables were included to provide a more comprehensive overview of the relationship between demographic variables and prediction market use.
A separate gender analysis was run to check the robustness of the preregistered model using biological sex.
Exploratory analyses also included a qualitative component.
The two open-response questions were analyzed using inductive content analysis (Elo & Kyngäs, 2008).

text.text: The fourth author conducted open coding on the responses and screened out responses that did not have enough information to be coded or did not answer the prompts provided (e.g.,"I don't know", or "I prefer Sportsbooks").
A codebook of preliminary themes were developed and reviewed by the research team to refine definitions and accurately reflect the data.
Following this, a second coder (fifth author) was invited to review the initial coding, recoding responses they disagreed with using the established coding scheme.
There was an excellent level (Kappa = 0.98) of agreement between the two reviewers.
The remaining disagreements were then resolved through consensus.
There were two deviations from this study's pre-registration.

First, ordinal regressions were used as a more appropriate alternative to bivariate linear regressions to test H3 and H4 because the outcome variable was ordinal, with unequal spacing between bins and unbounded upper and lower limits ("less than once a month" and "4 or more times a week").

Second, responses from the multiselect ethnicity item (White, Black, American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander, Native American or Indigenous, Hispanic or Latino, Middle Eastern, Biracial, Not listed; please specify) were recoded into six mutually exclusive categories (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic/Latino, Multi-racial, and Other) to facilitate the interpretability of the group comparisons within the regression analysis.

Prediction markets have grown rapidly in the past few years.
Although they are currently regulated as a financial product (event contracts), it has been argued that they can be seen as a form of gambling (Andrade & Newall, 2025; Johnson & Chan, 2026).
text.formatted: Although they are currently regulated as a financial product (event contracts), it has been argued that they can be seen as a form of gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Andrade & Newall, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Johnson & Chan, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, little is known about who uses prediction markets, their motivations, and links to traditional gambling.
The present study addressed this gap.

Taken together, our results provided support for our overall hypotheses that the convergence of prediction markets and gambling would extend beyond structural characteristics to gambling-related behaviours and psychological characteristics.
In other words, prediction markets may be a form of gambling masquerading as a financial product.
In support of H1, sports betting was significantly more popular than each other category of event contracts, with over 80% of participants having traded sports contracts.
These findings converge with market data, which suggest that sports contracts make up 78% of all trading volume on prediction markets (Kalshi; Radde, 2026).
text.formatted: These findings converge with market data, which suggest that sports contracts make up 78% of all trading volume on prediction markets (Kalshi; <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Radde, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While the wisdom of the crowds has been argued to have some societal benefits as a way to form probability estimates of future economic events, population perceptions of arbitrary events, like who is going to win the Superbowl are of little consequence to the economy.
Instead, the results of our study suggest that prediction markets primarily provide a different way to wager on sports.
The majority of prediction market users (84.0%) in our sample also engaged in traditional gambling and this proportion was shown to be significantly greater than 50%, which supported H2.
Furthermore, sports betting was the most commonly reported gambling activity.

Notably, the present study was advertised as a study on financial behaviours rather than self-selecting for participants who used prediction markets or engaged in gambling and consequently, we did not self-select for sports bettors.
Taken together, prediction markets appear to be primarily a vehicle for facilitating sports betting even in US states that have not legalised it.

Providing support for the aforementioned supposition, prediction markets were significantly more likely to be perceived to be a form of gambling (M = 8.27) rather than as a form of financial trading (M = 5.70; t(937) = 19.72, d = 0.64).

This finding is notable given our sample consisted of participants who primarily engaged in all three activities and thus could provide a direct comparison of prediction markets to gambling and financial trading.
The stock market is known by economists as a "positive sum" game, since the consequent spreading of risk across the economy can benefit both companies and individual investors.
By comparison, both gambling and prediction markets are "zero sum" games, where one person can win only at another person's loss.

Participants therefore appeared more aligned with economists in how they perceived prediction markets, rather than financial regulators who have classified prediction markets as financial transactions.

Our overall hypothesis (H3) that greater frequency of trading on frequency markets will resemble the demographic, psychological, and mental health and substance use patterns seen in sports betting was supported in several ways.

Greater frequency prediction market use was significantly associated with being male, younger age, having a great financially focused selfconcept, impulsivity, psychological distress and substance use.
These findings are not surprising given that sports betting was the most commonly traded event contract on prediction markets and the most commonly engaged form of gambling.

Future research that examines whether prediction market users who trade on non-sporting events also demonstrate a similar behavioural and psychological profile to individuals who gamble would be highly informative.
In regards to gambling related risk and harms, our hypothesis (H4) was supported, with the exception of gambling fallacies.

Specifically, greater frequency of trading on prediction markets was significantly associated with higher odds of problem gambling severity and lower dimensions of positive play (honesty, pre-commitment, personal responsibility and gambling literacy).
The null effects regarding gambling fallacies have several potential explanations.

First, the items used in this scale probe mistaken thoughts regarding conventional gambling products like slot machines and lottery tickets (Leonard & Williams, 2016), whereas we adapted the PPS to specifically probe behaviours and beliefs related to prediction markets.
text.formatted: First, the items used in this scale probe mistaken thoughts regarding conventional gambling products like slot machines and lottery tickets <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Leonard & Williams, 2016)</ref>, whereas we adapted the PPS to specifically probe behaviours and beliefs related to prediction markets.

text.text: It may be that prediction markets promote unique fallacies compared to the fallacies involved in conventional gambling products.

Second, while gambling fallacies have long been thought of as a key driver of problematic gambling, more recent longitudinal and experimental research has cast doubt on this causal relationship (Eben et al., 2026; Leonard et al., 2021).

text.text: Our exploratory results regarding motivations for trading on prediction markets further support the notion that they may be conceptualized as a form of gambling.
Financial motivations were the most commonly endorsed reason for trading on prediction markets in both the quantitative and qualitative analyses.
Financial motives are also a common motivation for engaging in gambling and have been robustly linked to problem gambling severity (Dias et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Financial motives are also a common motivation for engaging in gambling and have been robustly linked to problem gambling severity <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Dias et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Prediction markets also use similar advertisement tactics to traditional sports books such as financial incentives (e.g., sign-up bonus) to attract new users, further blurring the lines of gambling.

Furthermore, financial motivations, in particular related to perceived rate or return or more favourable odds, were a commonly reported reason for choosing prediction markets over traditional sports books.
Participants also drew direct parallels to gambling, noting that prediction markets fulfilled their pre-existing desires to gamble.
In contrast, motivations for using prediction markets as a source of information (i.e., wisdom of the crowds) were less commonly mentioned than motivations that aligned with traditional gambling.
Our qualitative results clarified and extended the quantitative findings in numerous ways.

For example, participants consistently described financial gain as a top motivation for using prediction markets and perceived greater financial returns on prediction markets over other sports betting platforms, converging with the quantitative associations between a financially focused self-concept and more frequent trading.

Second, participants described prediction markets as fulfilling a desire to gamble, aligning with the quantitative findings that most participants who used prediction markets also engaged in gambling.

Such findings echo preliminary evidence that prediction market usage is associated with gambling (Mastromartino, 2026) and suggest that the psychological profile of those who use prediction markets aligns with those who also engage in gambling.
text.formatted: Such findings echo preliminary evidence that prediction market usage is associated with gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Mastromartino, 2026)</ref> and suggest that the psychological profile of those who use prediction markets aligns with those who also engage in gambling.

text.text: Qualitative results also demonstrated additional nuance in the rationale of using prediction markets over traditional sportsbooks websites, with participants highlighting the variety of gambling options as a reason they specifically chose prediction markets, and describing prediction markets as having enhanced user interface and overall experience when compared to sportsbook.
Despite this, quantitative results indicated that participants used prediction markets most frequently for sports betting.

These findings suggest that the appeal of prediction markets may extend beyond the predominant categories that players bet on, and that prediction markets may be viewed as enhanced sports betting platforms in terms of their visual appeal and interface when compared to sportsbooks.

text.text: These findings may have important implications for regulation and policy.

Chiefly, though prediction markets position themselves as being a form of financial trading, users of prediction markets clearly understand them to be a type of gambling more than a type of financial trading.
Prediction markets are legally accessible from the age of 18, whereas sports betting is legally available from the age of 21.
Closing this regulatory gap is important given that young adults are at elevated risk of problematic gambling (Dellosa & Browne, 2024).
text.formatted: Closing this regulatory gap is important given that young adults are at elevated risk of problematic gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dellosa & Browne, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In fact, 3.1% of our sample were under the age of 21, and the lack of restrictions related to age were mentioned as a motivation for engaging in prediction markets.
Concerns around this appeal and accessibility to young people have been echoed in recent research (Chung, 2026).
text.formatted: Concerns around this appeal and accessibility to young people have been echoed in recent research <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Chung, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Prediction markets have also effectively facilitated sports betting in states that have not chosen to legalise it, and policymakers may also want to consider closing this regulatory loophole (Newall, 2026).

text.text: Additionally, prediction markets are not obligated to provide responsible gambling tools such as providing deposit limits, which again appears to be a consequential regulatory oversight given the findings reported here (Mastromartino, 2026).
text.formatted: Additionally, prediction markets are not obligated to provide responsible gambling tools such as providing deposit limits, which again appears to be a consequential regulatory oversight given the findings reported here <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Mastromartino, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, individuals who self-exclude from traditional online gambling sites could then turn to prediction markets to place bets (Allyn, 2026b).
text.formatted: Indeed, individuals who self-exclude from traditional online gambling sites could then turn to prediction markets to place bets <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Allyn, 2026b)</ref>.

text.text: Other measures that should be considered include the provision of warnings and information on prediction market adverts and platforms regarding the risk of problematic gambling.
Several limitations are worth noting.
The cross-sectional nature of the study precludes examining temporal links between prediction markets and traditional gambling.
Future longitudinal studies that examine whether trading on prediction markets influences transition to traditional gambling or vice versa would be informative.
Secondly, frequency and expenditure of both prediction market trading and gambling were assessed via retrospective self-reports, which may be susceptible to recall bias (Heirene et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Secondly, frequency and expenditure of both prediction market trading and gambling were assessed via retrospective self-reports, which may be susceptible to recall bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Heirene et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Replication of our results with objective data via account data or ecological momentary assessments would provide further confidence in these findings.
Lastly, our sample was recruited from Prolific, which may limit generalizability of our results compared to population-representative samples (Pickering & Blaszczynski, 2021).

text.text: Prediction markets have made it possible for individuals to wager money on anything from the weather, politics, and sports, to how many times Elon Musk will post on X in a day.
This "gamblification" of life has raised concerns that prediction markets are a form of gambling in disguise (Andrade & Newall, 2025).

text.text: Our results provide empirical support for this concern.
Specifically, prediction market users overlapped considerably in behaviours, motivations, psychological characteristics, and gambling-related risk and harms with individuals who gamble.
Indeed, despite being regulated as a financial product, prediction market users perceive trading on event contracts to be a form of gambling more so than financial trading.
Taken together, our results suggest that prediction markets could be considered a form of gambling in disguise and should be regulated as such.

text.text: Participants consistently reported financial gain as a motivation for using prediction markets and noted the perceived increased financial gain that they received by using prediction markets over sports betting platforms.
Qualitative results were complementary to the quantitative findings, highlighting the importance of finances in the motivations and profile of those who use prediction markets.
Most participants reported gambling in addition to trading on prediction markets.

Participants reported the desire to gamble as a motivation to use PMs, and that the lack of restrictions surrounding prediction markets allowed them to gamble in ways they were otherwise legally inaccessible to them.
Qualitative and quantitative results converged to demonstrate the relationship between prediction markets and gambling.
When asked about motivations for trading on prediction markets, the highest reported motivations were financial motives, followed by accomplishment and positive emotions.
Participants reported experiencing a "thrill" or positive sensations when using prediction markets, which served as a motivation for participants to engage in them.
Participants also cited competitive validation, referring to instances where they felt satisfaction in being correct or accurate in their predictions, as a motivation to use prediction markets.
Quantitative and qualitative results converge to suggest that affective rewards, specifically positive emotions and a sense of accomplishment, are motivators for prediction market use.
Participants reported a variety of categories they traded on in prediction markets, including sports (81.20%), financial markets (55.2%), and domestic policies (41.8%).

Participants reported that their motivation for using prediction markets were due to the flexibility of betting options, most importantly, the ability to bet on different categories as a reason why they used prediction markets over traditional sports betting platforms.
Quantitative and qualitative findings diverged regarding the emphasis of sports betting.

Although sports was the most frequently reported betting category quantitatively, qualitative findings highlighted the diversity of available betting options as a key motivation for choosing prediction markets over traditional sports betting platforms.
Qualitative Findings Interpretation Participants most often used prediction markets to trade on sports event contracts.

Findings suggest that prediction markets may be viewed as elevated sports betting platforms and particularly attractive to individuals who wish to bet on sports.
